# <img src="./.github/img/modern-web-guidance.svg" alt="Modern Web Guidance" width="30" height="30"> Modern Web Guidance (Source)

This repo is the source repository for [GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance) and includes the code and documentation for authoring, calibrating, and evaluating its contents.

[**Modern Web Guidance**](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) and [GOVERNANCE.md](./GOVERNANCE.md) for how we work on the project and orientation of the codebase.

---

*Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.*

[Documentation](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) · [Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/) · [Source Code](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src) · [Report an Issue](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues)

## <img src="https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/raw/main/.github/img/terminal.svg" width="24" height="24" style="vertical-align: middle; margin-right: 4px;"> Quickstart

```shell
npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
```

This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See [Alternative Installation Methods](#-alternative-installation-methods) below.

#### Try it out (without installing)

```shell
# Search for relevant guides
npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop"

# Retrieve a guide by ID
npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer"

# Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize
npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan .
```

## <img src="https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/raw/main/.github/img/lightbulb.svg" width="24" height="24" style="vertical-align: middle; margin-right: 4px;"> Why?

Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions.

Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code.

**Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap.** Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on:
* **Modern Browser APIs**: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse.
* **Performance & Accessibility**: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances.
* **Responsible Fallbacks**: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries.

## <img src="https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/raw/main/.github/img/package.svg" width="24" height="24" style="vertical-align: middle; margin-right: 4px;"> What's Included?

We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are **designed to be token-efficient**; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know.

README

# Codex Security

Codex Security helps you find, investigate, and fix vulnerabilities in your code.
Use its security workflows in Codex, or automate them with the
`@openai/codex-security` CLI and TypeScript SDK.

- **In Codex:** [choose a security workflow](docs/agent-workflows.md).
- **In a terminal:** [install the CLI and scan your repository](#quick-start).
- **In automation:** use the [TypeScript SDK](#typescript-sdk) or
  [GitHub Action](#github-actions).

## Features

- Scan repositories, selected paths, or Git changes. Deep scans repeat Standard scans and return their deduplicated findings.
- Validate candidate findings, generate patches, and verify existing fixes.
- Draft `SECURITY.md` policies and save threat models for later review.
- Browse saved scans and findings, identify duplicates, assess severity against
  your own rubric, and suggest owners from source and Git history.
- Preview third-party scanner findings, save them locally, or publish supported reports to Codex Security Cloud. [Scanner import guides](docs/scanner-imports/README.md).
- Track findings in Linear, Jira, or GitHub, publish completed scans, or export SARIF, JSON, and CSV. [Integration workflows](docs/plugin-connectors.md).
- Automate scans across repositories or project components, including in CI and
  containers.

## Use in Codex

Open your repository in a Codex session with the Codex Security plugin enabled,
then ask:

> Run a Codex Security scan on this repository, focusing on authentication and
> authorization. Return the saved report, source evidence, and coverage limits.

A completed scan saves a report and findings. Read the report for source
evidence and exclusions, then request a patch or ask Codex to verify an
existing fix. See the [agent workflow guide](docs/agent-workflows.md) for setup,
task selection, and recovery.

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 22.13.0+ within 22.x, or Node.js 24.x or 26.x, and Python 3.10+.
Python 3.10 also requires `tomli`.

Install the CLI globally and sign in:

```bash
npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login
```

Run your first scan from the repository directory:

```bash
cs scan .
```

When the scan completes, open the Markdown file at the **REPORT** path in the
terminal. Run `cs scans show` from the same repository to find its latest
completed scan again. See [scan scope and follow-up work](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#understand-scan-scope-and-follow-up-work)
for how to interpret exclusions in the report.

`cs` and `codex-security` run the same CLI. If the short name conflicts with
another command, use `codex-security`. To skip the global install, or if npm
reports an `EEXIST` conflict, use `npx @openai/codex-security` in place of
`cs` for both login and scanning.

For CI, set `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `CODEX_API_KEY` in the scan process's environment.
For a headless machine, see [device or SSH login](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#authentication).

### Scan options

Choose a scope and scan mode:

```bash
# Scan selected paths.
cs scan . --path src --path tests

# Scan committed changes from a base revision to HEAD.
cs scan . --diff origin/main

# Run a deep scan of the repository.
cs scan . --mode deep
```

Use `cs scan . --max-time 15` for an advisory 15-minute Standard investigation
allowance. See [investigation time](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#set-investigation-time)
for timing semantics and Deep Scan limits.

Use `cs --help` to browse commands, or `cs scan --help`
for scan options, cost limits, and patching after a scan.

For an application spread across repositories, see
[review one system across repositories](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#review-one-system-across-repositories).
Use [bulk scans](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#bulk-scans) for independent repository
reviews in one resumable campaign.

Scans use existing root and component `SECURITY.md` guidance. To write or
revise it, see [Generate SECURITY.md](#generate-securitymd).

Some cybersecurity requests and protected findings require
[Trusted Access for Cyber](https://chatgpt.com/cyber). For accounts with Daybreak
access, see [Daybreak opt-in](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#daybreak-opt-in) for the
Codex toggle and [Cyber access programs](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#select-a-cyber-access-program)
to select a program explicitly.

## TypeScript SDK

Install the package locally in your TypeScript project:

```bash
npm install @openai/codex-security
```

Then import it:

```ts
import { CodexSecurity } from "@openai/codex-security";

const security = new CodexSecurity();

try {
  const result = await security.run("/path/to/repository");
  console.log(result.reportPath);
} finally {
  await security.close();
}
```

The [SDK guide](sdk/typescript/docs/sdk.md) includes deep-scan configuration,
validation, severity classification, owner suggestions, and result handling.

Linked Git worktrees share scan history and saved findings when they use the same
Codex Security state directory. Keep `CODEX_SECURITY_STATE_DIR` stable to retain
that shared history and sign-in scope. See the [scan history guide](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#scan-history-and-reruns).

## Read existing Cloud findings

When Codex Security Cloud is available to your account, the Security plugin's
`$cloud-findings` skill can read findings, reports, recorded assignment and
verification, and scan status in Codex desktop or the Codex CLI. Cloud is an
optional connection; local scans work without it.

See [Cloud connection setup and CLI reads](sdk/typescript/docs/sdk.md#read-existing-cloud-findings)
for authentication requirements and a read-only example.

## Generate SECURITY.md

Use `policy` to draft a new `SECURITY.md` or update an existing one. Use `--path`
to select a component:

```bash
cs policy .
cs policy . --path services/api --knowledge-base architecture.md
```

The command saves its draft outside the repository and leaves existing files
unchanged. Review the diff and notes, edit the draft, then copy only `SECURITY.md`
to the displayed **Policy target**. Keep the saved architecture and threat-model
documents outside the repository.

Scans already use root and component `SECURITY.md` files. Keep your current policy
if it needs no changes. When updating it, preserve its vulnerability-reporting
instructions. If the command says the policy is already up to date, no copy is
needed.

Files at `.github/SECURITY.md` or `docs/SECURITY.md` often contain reporting
instructions. Preserve them when drafting a policy; those locations do not
automatically provide repository-wide scan guidance. See the
[policy guide](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#generate-a-security-policy) for policy
locations, unanswered questions, saved artifacts, and SDK usage.

## Save and export threat models

Scans and policy generation save threat models with their results. Export a saved
model without starting another analysis:

```bash
cs export --scan SCAN_ID --artifact threat-model --output threatmodel.md
```

Omit `--scan` to use the current repository's latest completed scan. The
[export guide](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#exports-and-ci) also covers findings,
SARIF output for CI, and the offline TypeScript API. For ServiceNow Application
Vulnerability Response, see [Export findings for ServiceNow](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#export-findings-for-servicenow).

## GitHub Actions

To run a weekly repository scan on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu:

1. Add an OpenAI API key as the repository secret `CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY`.
2. Copy the [weekly workflow](github-action/examples/repository.yml) to
   `.github/workflows/codex-security.yml`. Replace `REPLACE_WITH_REVIEWED_COMMIT`
   with the reviewed distribution commit SHA from an Action release.
3. To try the workflow before the next scheduled run, open **Actions → Codex
   Security repository → Run workflow**.

The example uses an estimated $5 limit per scan and reports findings without
failing the job. Requests in progress can exceed the limit. For a severity
threshold, pull request checks, or runner requirements, see the
[Action guide](github-action/README.md). For eligible accounts, see
[Daybreak access](github-action/README.md#daybreak-access-and-refusals).

## Containerized bulk scans

Scan a list of repositories with the included Docker Compose configuration,
which keeps results and authentication between runs. See the
[container quick start](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#containerized-bulk-scans).
The [workflow runner](docker/README.md#workflow-runner) runs individual CLI stages
in containers and can connect to a separately deployed findings service.

## Findings storage and deduplication

The [findings guide](sdk/typescript/docs/findings-service.md) covers local
storage, deduplication, and compatibility with independently operated endpoints
through `publish scan --to custom` and explicit `--findings-url`. The local
`serve` command and browser dashboard have been removed; existing databases and
scan artifacts remain available.

## Other providers

Scans support OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference. Bedrock uses
AWS credentials and does not require a separate OpenAI login. See
[Bedrock setup](docs/bedrock.md) for AWS profiles, regions, and model access.

For OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference, set the provider's API key and choose a supported
model. See [provider configuration](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#native-command-authentication-and-other-providers)
for examples.

## Documentation

- [Online documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/security/cli)
- [Agent workflows and recovery](docs/agent-workflows.md)
- [CLI reference](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md)
- [Imported finding identity and evidence](docs/scanner-imports/schema-guide.md)
- [Project configuration](docs/project-configuration.md)
- [Examples](examples/README.md)

To report a vulnerability privately, follow the [security policy](SECURITY.md).

**It plugs directly into your agent** through plugins, hooks and commands. When the agent proposes a decision, plan, html, or finishes working, the app opens in your browser and you mark it up, comment, and send feedback directly to the agent for it to act on it.

<table>
<tr>
<td width="40%" valign="middle">

### Review documents, plans, and agent messages

Annotate plans, specs, messages, html, then send the feedback to your agent. 

<p><strong>Demo:</strong> <a href="https://youtu.be/XqFun9XCXPw">Plan review with Pi</a></p>

</td>

</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td width="40%" valign="middle">

### Code Review

Review local changes or remote PRs. Comment on diffs, suggest code. Your comments go back to the agent. Works with Git, GitButler, Jujutsu (`jj`), Perforce (`p4`), GitHub, and GitLab.

</td>
<td width="60%">

<p align="center">

</p>

## Annotate HTML Artifacts

<p align="center">
  <img src=".github/assets/html.webp" alt="Annotating a rendered HTML artifact" width="720" />
</p>

## Plannotator Inbox

<p align="center">
  <a href="https://plannotator.ai/inbox/">
    <picture>
      <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset=".github/assets/inbox-dark.webp" />

The Plannotator Inbox is one local window where your agents leave you messages, questions, files, and guided reviews while they keep working. Answer a question with a click, annotate a file, and press Send when you can. Nothing holds an agent session open while you do, and your reply goes back to the session that asked.

```
plannotator inbox
```

Claude Code, Pi, and OpenCode connect through Plannotator's plugins, and your replies arrive as their next turn. Any other agent reaches it over MCP with `plannotator inbox mcp`, and `plannotator inbox --help` is the guide an agent reads. [Watch the demo](https://plannotator.ai/assets/inbox-film.mp4) · [More on the Inbox](https://plannotator.ai/inbox/) · [Docs](https://plannotator.ai/docs/reference/inbox/)

## Herdr Annotate: Plannotator in the Terminal

<p align="center">
  <a href="https://github.com/plannotator/herdr-annotate">
    <img src=".github/assets/herdr-annotate-banner.svg" alt="Herdr Annotate" width="300" align="middle" />
  </a>
    
  <img src=".github/assets/herdr-annotate.png" alt="Plannotator TUI annotating a markdown folder in the terminal" width="480" align="middle" />
</p>

[Herdr Annotate](https://github.com/plannotator/herdr-annotate) brings Plannotator-style review to the terminal: annotate terminal text, review whole Markdown documents and your coding agent's replies inside [Herdr](https://herdr.dev), and send the feedback straight back to the agent as its next message. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Copilot CLI, and Droid replies. Annotations are saved in the Plannotator data directory, so terminal reviews and app reviews compound.

```
herdr plugin install plannotator/herdr-annotate
```

Prefer it standalone? [Plannotator TUI](https://github.com/plannotator/plannotator-tui) powers the document review and runs without Herdr: `brew install plannotator/tap/plannotator-tui`.

---

## Commands

<sub>On Codex, swap the slash commands for `!plannotator …` (e.g. `!plannotator review`) or the `$plannotator-*` skills.</sub>

### Annotate

```
/plannotator-annotate README.md                  # Local markdown file
/plannotator-annotate src/                       # Browse and annotate files in a folder
/plannotator-annotate https://docs.rs/…          # Fetch and annotate any URL
/plannotator-annotate report.html --render-html  # Render HTML as-is instead of converting
/plannotator-last                                # Annotate the agent's last message
```

Need a realistic document to try? Copy the [product requirements document template and filled example](https://docs.plannotator.ai/templates/product-requirements-document) as Markdown.

### Code review

```
/plannotator-review                    # Review uncommitted changes
/plannotator-review <github-pr-url>    # Review a GitHub pull request
/plannotator-review <gitlab-mr-url>    # Review a GitLab merge request
plannotator review --gitbutler         # Review an active GitButler workspace
plannotator review --patch-file reading.diff # Review a static caller-supplied unified diff
```

GitButler users can review the whole workspace, one stack, or one branch layer. See the [GitButler workflow guide](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/workflows/gitbutler).

### Plan mode

No command needed. Plan mode is wired in through each harness's hooks. Any time your agent creates a plan, the markdown review surface opens for you.

### CLI

```
plannotator sessions                   # List active Plannotator sessions
plannotator sessions --open 1          # Reopen a session in the browser
plannotator archive                    # Browse saved plan decisions read-only
```

---

## Privacy and network behavior

Plannotator does not collect usage telemetry or analytics. Plans, diffs, annotations, drafts, history, and configuration stay local by default.

Each plan review, annotate, archive, share-portal, and code-review app surface checks GitHub for the latest Plannotator release when it loads. This sends no plan or review content and gives the Plannotator project owner no usage analytics, although GitHub receives an ordinary request. There is currently no opt-out setting for the release check. Local Git code review can also query the configured `origin` with `git ls-remote` to detect the default branch and a stale baseline; it does not send the local diff. That remote query runs when the review opens, when the page loads its diff, when you switch the diff type or base (including the "Diff out of date · Refresh" button), and when you press Fetch — never on a timer, so an idle review page makes no network calls. Turn it off entirely with `plannotator review --no-git-remote-check`, `PLANNOTATOR_GIT_REMOTE_CHECK=0`, or `{ "gitRemoteCheck": false }` in `~/.plannotator/config.json`; the compare target then comes from local refs only and the "behind GitHub" banner never appears.

Content leaves the local workflow only when a network feature needs it:

- URL annotation fetches the requested site, through Jina Reader by default for public pages or directly when Jina is disabled or unavailable.
- GitHub and GitLab review uses your authenticated CLI and Git remote to retrieve PR or MR data.
- Ask AI and review agents send the selected question and relevant plan, document, repository, or diff context to your configured provider. When Ask AI is answered by the agent session that opened Plannotator ("Ask this session"), the question goes to that session instead.
- Sharing sends the complete link to whoever or whatever service you use to deliver it. Encrypted short links upload ciphertext to the paste service.
- Workspaces is a separate hosted product, so the open source app's local-storage model does not apply to content placed there.

The [privacy policy](https://plannotator.ai/privacy) documents these boundaries and the hosted website and waitlist data.

---

## Link sharing

Open source asynchronous link sharing remains available for compatibility but is moving to deprecated support. Workspaces is the primary direction for team sharing. No removal date has been announced.

<p align="center">
  <a href="https://room.plannotator.ai/">
    <img src=".github/assets/sharing.png" alt="Sharing portal with upload options" width="720" />
  </a>
</p>

<p align="center">
  <sub>Legacy link-sharing demo: <a href="https://room.plannotator.ai/">room.plannotator.ai</a></sub>
</p>

<p align="center">
  <a href="https://plannotator.ai/workspaces">
    <img src=".github/assets/workspaces-cta.svg" alt="Workspaces is the team-sharing direction. Join the waitlist." height="44" />
  </a>
</p>

Share a plan with a teammate and they can annotate it themselves. Import their feedback and send it straight back to your agent.

**Small markdown shares** are compressed into the URL fragment. The fragment is not included in the browser's request to the share portal, but it is not encrypted. Anyone or any messaging service with the complete link can read the shared content. The portal host still receives ordinary request metadata.

**Large markdown and raw HTML shares** use a short-link service. The share payload is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before upload, the server stores only ciphertext, and the key is kept in the URL fragment rather than sent in the paste request. Anyone with the complete link can decrypt it. Hosted pastes expire after 7 days.

Same model as [PrivateBin](https://privatebin.info/). The paste service is [self-hostable](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/workflows/sharing).

Sharing can be disabled entirely with `PLANNOTATOR_SHARE=disabled`.

[Workspaces](https://plannotator.ai/workspaces) is the primary path for hosted team collaboration.

---

## Install

One installer covers almost every agent. It installs the `plannotator` binary, auto-detects your installed agents, and configures hooks, skills, and slash commands for each:

```bash
# macOS / Linux / WSL
curl -fsSL https://plannotator.ai/install.sh | bash
```

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
irm https://plannotator.ai/install.ps1 | iex
```

The installer downloads the binary from GitHub Releases. A full install can also contact GitHub for release resolution and agent files, Ataraxy-Labs/sem for the optional `sem` sidecar, and npm for Pi, selected extra skills, or the managed agent-terminal runtime. Pinning `--version` skips only GitHub API release resolution, not the release download. See the [privacy policy](https://plannotator.ai/privacy) for the complete network boundaries.

Want just the binary and nothing else? Pass `--minimal` (or export `PLANNOTATOR_MINIMAL=1`) to install only the `plannotator` binary to `~/.local/bin`, skipping every skill, hook, slash command, and per-agent config:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://plannotator.ai/install.sh | bash -s -- --minimal
```

Then finish the step for your agent:

| Agent | After the installer | Details |
|---|---|---|
| **Amp** | Copy [`plannotator.ts`](apps/amp-plugin/plannotator.ts) into `~/.config/amp/plugins/`, then `plugins: reload`. Workflows live in the command palette. | [README](apps/amp-plugin/README.md) |
| **Claude Code** | `/plugin marketplace add backnotprop/plannotator`, then `/plugin install plannotator@plannotator`. Restart Claude Code. | [README](apps/hook/README.md) |
| **Codex** | Nothing. Plan review is enabled automatically via Codex's experimental `Stop` hook (macOS/Linux/WSL; on native Windows, Codex hooks are experimental and the installer prints manual setup steps). `$plannotator-review`, `$plannotator-annotate`, and `$plannotator-last` skills included. | [README](apps/codex/README.md) |
| **Copilot CLI** | `/plugin marketplace add backnotprop/plannotator`, then `/plugin install plannotator-copilot@plannotator`. Restart. Plan review activates in plan mode (`Shift+Tab`). | [README](apps/copilot/README.md) |
| **DeepSeek Harness** | Add `@plannotator/dsh` on DSH's Plugins page, or run `dsh plugin --profile <profile> add @plannotator/dsh`. Plan review opens on `exit_plan_mode`. The plugin adds `/plannotator-review`, `/plannotator-annotate` and `/plannotator-last`, which open without blocking the session. | [README](apps/dsh-plugin/README.md) |
| **Droid** | `droid plugin marketplace add https://github.com/backnotprop/plannotator`, then `droid plugin install plannotator@plannotator`. Commands only, no plan interception yet. | [README](apps/droid-plugin/README.md) |
| **Gemini CLI** | Nothing. The hook, policy, and slash commands are configured automatically. Requires Gemini CLI 0.36.0+. | [README](apps/gemini/README.md) |
| **Kiro CLI** | Nothing. Skills and an example agent are installed automatically. Try `kiro-cli chat --agent plannotator`. | [README](apps/kiro-cli/README.md) |
| **OpenCode** | Add `"plugin": ["@plannotator/opencode@latest"]` to `opencode.json`. Restart OpenCode. | [README](apps/opencode-plugin/README.md) |
| **Pi** | Skip the installer. Just `pi install npm:@plannotator/pi-extension`. Start Pi with `--plan`, or toggle with `/plannotator-plan-mode`. | [README](apps/pi-extension/README.md) |
| **T3 Code** | For Claude threads in T3: run `plannotator t3 --help` and follow its two steps (sign in to T3 once, add the `--t3` MCP entry). Your Inbox replies then arrive in the thread as new turns. | [README](packages/t3-code/README.md) |

**Updating:** run the installer again for the binary and slash commands. It also updates an installed Claude Code plugin when the `claude` command is on your PATH (opt out with `--skip-claude-plugin`); otherwise run `claude plugin marketplace update plannotator`, then `claude plugin update plannotator@plannotator`, then restart Claude Code (refreshing the marketplace alone does not update the plugin). Pi: `pi update --extensions` (a plain `pi update` updates only Pi).

On Claude Code 2.1.287 or newer, plan review, code review and annotate don't make Claude wait: Claude ends its turn and your decision arrives later as a message. Set `PLANNOTATOR_CLAUDE_MOD=0` to go back to the classic flow.

Full walkthroughs live in the [installation docs](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/start/installation).

### Uninstall

The safe default removes recognized Plannotator-installed components and keeps
your local plans, history, drafts, guides, and settings:

```bash
plannotator uninstall
```

Use `--purge` for a full removal of known local Plannotator data as well:

```bash
plannotator uninstall --purge
```

Purge requires typing `purge` at the prompt and explains that the data is
local-only: it is not stored on a Plannotator server and cannot be recovered.
For automation, pass `--yes` (or `-y`); non-interactive removal refuses to run
without it. Use `--dry-run` to preview recognized work without making changes.
Host integrations are always part of uninstall. If a broken or unavailable
host prevents safe cleanup, the command names the blocking plugin manager or
configuration, gives exact manual cleanup instructions, and stops before
deleting the binary. Complete that cleanup and rerun uninstall.
It also keeps the binary when an agent's config file can't be read (another
tool's too), or when a hook it did not install still runs Plannotator. The
error names the file, the tool, and what to do. A `plannotator-inbox` entry
you added yourself, or a Claude Code or Droid plugin installed for one project,
is named with how to remove it and does not keep the binary.
These mechanics keep the ordinary confirmation default-negative, make the
irreversible outcome require a stronger explicit word, and still give package
managers and scripts a conventional non-interactive flag.

The command covers the conventional macOS, Linux, WSL, and Windows binary
locations; the managed `sem` sidecar and agent-terminal runtime; installer
skills, commands, hooks, policies, caches, and recognizable Amp/Kiro files; and
detected Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Droid, Pi, and VS Code installations through
their host CLIs. Shared JSONC settings are edited surgically, while strict JSON
updates preserve the file's indentation, line endings, and trailing-newline
style. Custom
or unrecognized files, separately installed optional skills, project-local
integrations, external plan-save locations, and invalid configs are preserved
(malformed host config is a fail-safe error). If cleanup reports an error,
the CLI remains available for a safe retry, and its Windows PATH entry is
retained or restored when possible. If PATH restoration itself fails, the
output gives the full CLI path for retry and asks for manual PATH repair.
For safety, purge refuses filesystem roots, the home directory, the shared
temporary directory, symlinked data directories, and non-directory data paths.
Existing paths are compared by filesystem identity, so case aliases, symlinks,
hardlinks, and bind mounts cannot bypass the root/home/ancestor checks.
That identity and every containment guard are revalidated after awaited host
commands, immediately before the synchronous data-removal block; a replaced
data directory is refused without touching either the old or replacement data.
If your dedicated data directory is symlinked, point `PLANNOTATOR_DATA_DIR` at
its resolved target and retry.

If you installed only the standalone Pi extension and do not have the
`plannotator` CLI, use `pi remove npm:@plannotator/pi-extension`.

README

# Chrome DevTools for agents

[![npm chrome-devtools-mcp package](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/chrome-devtools-mcp.svg)](https://npmjs.org/package/chrome-devtools-mcp)

Chrome DevTools for agents (`chrome-devtools-mcp`) lets your coding agent (such as Antigravity, Claude, Cursor or Copilot)
control and inspect a live Chrome browser. It is available as a
Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server and as a [CLI][cli]. Both give your AI
coding assistant access to the full power of Chrome DevTools for reliable
automation, in-depth debugging, and performance analysis.

[Tool reference][tool-reference] | [CLI][cli] | [Skills][skills] | [Changelog][changelog] | [Contributing][contributing] | [Troubleshooting][troubleshooting] | [Design Principles][design-principles]

## Key features

- **Get performance insights**: Uses [Chrome
  DevTools](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/devtools-frontend) to record
  traces and extract actionable performance insights.
- **Advanced browser debugging**: Analyze network requests, take screenshots and
  check browser console messages (with source-mapped stack traces).
- **Reliable automation**. Uses
  [puppeteer](https://github.com/puppeteer/puppeteer) to automate actions in
  Chrome and automatically wait for action results.

## Disclaimers

`chrome-devtools-mcp` exposes content of the browser instance to the MCP clients
allowing them to inspect, debug, and modify any data in the browser or DevTools.
Avoid sharing sensitive or personal information that you don't want to share with
MCP clients.

`chrome-devtools-mcp` officially supports Google Chrome and [Chrome for Testing](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-for-testing/) only.
Other Chromium-based browsers may work, but this is not guaranteed, and you may encounter unexpected behavior. Use at your own discretion.
We are committed to providing fixes and support for the latest version of [Extended Stable Chrome](https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule).

Performance tools may send trace URLs to the Google CrUX API to fetch real-user
experience data. This helps provide a holistic performance picture by
presenting field data alongside lab data. This data is collected by the [Chrome
User Experience Report (CrUX)](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/crux). To disable
this, run with the `--no-performance-crux` flag.

## **Usage statistics**

Google collects usage statistics (such as tool invocation success rates, latency, and environment information) to improve the reliability and performance of Chrome DevTools MCP.

Data collection is **enabled by default**. You can opt-out by passing the `--no-usage-statistics` flag when starting the server:

```json
"args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest", "--no-usage-statistics"]
```

Google handles this data in accordance with the [Google Privacy Policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy).

Google's collection of usage statistics for Chrome DevTools MCP is independent from the Chrome browser's usage statistics. Opting out of Chrome metrics does not automatically opt you out of this tool, and vice-versa.

Collection is disabled if `CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_USAGE_STATISTICS` or `CI` env variables are set.

## Update checks

By default, the server periodically checks the npm registry for updates and logs a notification when a newer version is available.
You can disable these update checks by setting the `CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_UPDATE_CHECKS` environment variable.

## Requirements

- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) [LTS](https://github.com/nodejs/Release#release-schedule) version.
- [Chrome](https://www.google.com/chrome/) current stable version or newer.
- [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/)

## Getting started

Add the following config to your MCP client:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "chrome-devtools": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
    }
  }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> Using `chrome-devtools-mcp@latest` ensures that your MCP client will always use the latest version of the Chrome DevTools MCP server.

### MCP Client configuration

For setup instructions specific to your editor or agent (e.g. Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code), please see our [Client Configurations Guide][client-configurations-guide].

### Your first prompt

Enter the following prompt in your MCP Client to check if everything is working:

```
Check the performance of https://developers.chrome.com
```

Your MCP client should open the browser and record a performance trace.

> [!NOTE]
> The MCP server will start the browser automatically once the MCP client uses a tool that requires a running browser instance. Connecting to the Chrome DevTools MCP server on its own will not automatically start the browser.

## CLI

The package also includes the `chrome-devtools` CLI. Use it to control the browser from your terminal without MCP:

```sh
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
chrome-devtools navigate_page 1 --url "https://developers.chrome.com"
chrome-devtools take_screenshot 1 --filePath screenshot.png
chrome-devtools stop
```

See the [CLI guide][cli] for all commands and options.

## Skills

The package includes [skills](./skills) that teach your agent how to use Chrome DevTools:

| Skill                                                     | Use it to                                       |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| [`chrome-devtools`](./skills/chrome-devtools)             | Debug and automate pages with the MCP tools.    |
| [`chrome-devtools-cli`](./skills/chrome-devtools-cli)     | Run the CLI and write shell scripts with it.    |
| [`a11y-debugging`](./skills/a11y-debugging)               | Audit and fix accessibility issues.             |
| [`cookie-debugging`](./skills/cookie-debugging)           | Debug cookies, sessions, and authentication.    |
| [`debug-optimize-lcp`](./skills/debug-optimize-lcp)       | Debug and improve Largest Contentful Paint.     |
| [`memory-leak-debugging`](./skills/memory-leak-debugging) | Find and fix memory leaks.                      |
| [`troubleshooting`](./skills/troubleshooting)             | Fix connection problems between MCP and Chrome. |

### Install skills as a plugin

A plugin installs the MCP server and all skills, including the CLI skill:

- **Claude Code:** Run `/plugin marketplace add ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp`, then `/plugin install chrome-devtools-mcp@chrome-devtools-plugins`.
- **Copilot / VS Code:** Run **Chat: Install Plugin From Source** and enter `ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp`.
- **Gemini CLI:** Run `gemini extensions install --auto-update https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp`.

See the [Client Configurations Guide][client-configurations-guide] for more information.

### Install skills manually

If your agent does not support plugins, copy the skill folders into the skills directory of your agent. The npm package contains the skills:

```sh
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
# Example for Claude Code. Use the skills directory of your agent.
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root -g)/chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli" ~/.claude/skills/
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The `chrome-devtools-cli` skill requires the CLI. Install the package globally before you use the skill.

### Keep skills up to date

Skills describe the tools of a specific version. Update the skills each time you update the MCP server or the CLI. Outdated skills can tell your agent to use tools or parameters that changed.

- **Plugins:** Use the update command of the plugin manager of your agent. The Gemini CLI command above enables automatic updates with `--auto-update`.
- **Manual installs:** Update the package, then copy the skill folders again:

```sh
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root -g)/chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli" ~/.claude/skills/
```

## Tools

If you run into any issues, checkout our [troubleshooting guide][troubleshooting].
See the full [Tool Reference][tool-reference] for a complete list of all supported MCP capabilities.

## Configuration

Find the complete list of server parameters (e.g., `--headless`, `--isolated`, `--slim`) and how to configure WebSocket connections in the [Configuration Guide][configuration-guide].

For basic browser tasks only, the `--slim` flag exposes a reduced set of tools. See the [Slim tool reference][slim-tool-reference].

## Advanced Usage

For advanced features such as handling concurrent sessions, persistent user data directories, using a custom or non-standard browser path (`--executablePath`), connecting to a running Chrome instance instead of starting a new one, or debugging on Android, see our [Advanced Usage Guide][advanced-usage-guide].

## Integrating as a browser subagent

If you are developing agentic tooling and want to provide an integrated browser subagent as part of your product, we recommend building on top of Chrome DevTools for agents.

For a reference implementation, see the [Gemini CLI browser agent documentation](https://geminicli.com/docs/core/subagents/#browser-agent).

### For your team

**OpenBot for Business** brings your agents into one workspace with company sign-in, tool permissions, approvals, and audit. Deploy on your infrastructure or work with our engineers on hosting and customization.

[**Get early access to OpenBot for Business →**](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=business&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [**Talk to an engineer**](https://open.bot/business) · [**Kubernetes setup**](#deploy-on-kubernetes)

[Web](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=web&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [iOS](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=ios&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [Android](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=android&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [Slack](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=slack&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [Teams](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=teams&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access)

## Your workspace. Your stack.

<div align="center">
<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="docs/assets/openbot-stack-dark.svg">
  <img src="docs/assets/openbot-stack-light.svg" alt="OpenBot's modular stack: an enterprise workspace over built-in or AG-UI agents, your models, MCP tools, configurable infrastructure, and deployment on your laptop or Kubernetes." width="90%">
</picture>
</div>

- **Choose your models.** Use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, or open models through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, hosted by a provider or on your own infrastructure. Keep your provider relationships and change models as your needs change.
- **Bring your agents.** Run built-in Bots in the OpenBot server, or connect your existing agents through AG-UI from any agent execution platform. Agents built with different stacks can work in the same workspace.
- **Make it yours.** Use the MIT-licensed template as-is, white-label it, or customize it deeply. AG-UI connects agents, MCP connects tools, and the frontends and backend can evolve independently.
- **Govern work across your team.** Company sign-in, roles, tool permissions, approvals, and audit apply across the workspace. Your agents use OpenBot's tools and computers under the same policies.
- **Get help deploying it.** CopilotKit's engineers can work with your team to deploy OpenBot, connect your systems, and automate parts of specific jobs.

[Connect your agent](#bring-your-own-agent) · [Configure models and tools](docs/configuration.md) · [Explore OpenBot for Business](https://open.bot/business)

## Built on CopilotKit and AG-UI

OpenBot is built on [CopilotKit](https://www.copilotkit.ai), which is [used in production by a majority of Fortune 500 companies](https://www.copilotkit.ai/blog/series-a).

**Your agent stack.** [AG-UI](https://docs.ag-ui.com/introduction#supported-integrations) has first-class integrations across the major agent frameworks and harnesses, including Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework and Agent Harness, Google ADK, AWS Strands, Oracle Agent Spec, LangChain, Mastra, Pydantic AI, Agno, and CrewAI. Many ship first-party support; [Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supports AG-UI directly](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-agui.html).

**Your execution platform.** Keep your agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Managed Agents, [Google's Agent Platform](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform), LangChain's Managed Deep Agents, [Microsoft Foundry Agent Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/hosted-agents), or your own infrastructure. Connect them to OpenBot through an AG-UI endpoint, using an adapter where needed. Your choice of agent platform stays independent of your workspace.

## Architecture

OpenBot has three parts. On your laptop, setup runs the backend and Intelligence for you. For a team, the Helm chart deploys both on Kubernetes in your own infrastructure.

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="docs/assets/architecture-overview-dark.svg">
  <img src="docs/assets/architecture-overview-light.svg" alt="Mac, Windows, web, iOS, Android, Slack, and Teams connect to the OpenBot backend. Built-in Bots in the server and your agents on any execution platform share an AG-UI lane. Computer execution uses Kubernetes by default or a compatible sandbox provider; tools use MCP and adapters. CopilotKit Intelligence runs alongside OpenBot on your infrastructure." width="100%">
</picture>

| Part | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **OpenBot frontends** | Mac, Windows, web, iOS, Android, Slack, and Teams connect people to the same workspace. Conversations, interactive results, computer view, and approvals adapt to each surface. [Choose a frontend](#getting-started). |
| **OpenBot backend** | Runs the workspace API and built-in Bots, connects external agents and tools, manages Bot computers, and enforces identity, permissions, action policies, and audit. Deploys on Kubernetes with PostgreSQL and persistent storage. |
| **CopilotKit Intelligence** | Durable conversations, memory, Automatic Learning, and enterprise governance services. Separately licensed; runs on Kubernetes alongside OpenBot. |

OpenBot enforces sign-in, tool permissions, action policies, and audit at its API, alongside Intelligence's platform services. Built-in Bots run in the OpenBot server; your own agents can run alongside OpenBot or on any agent execution platform. Both use AG-UI and can share the same workspace.

Computer execution is pluggable: use the default Kubernetes setup or connect a compatible external computer provider.

[Architecture details](docs/architecture.md) · [Services and ports](#services-and-ports) · [Kubernetes deployment](#deploy-on-kubernetes)

## Open source, local operation, and licensing

**The OpenBot application template is open source under the [MIT license](LICENSE).** You can fork, modify, and white-label it. It uses **CopilotKit Intelligence**, which is separately licensed and can run entirely on your own machine or infrastructure.

| Where you run it | CopilotKit Intelligence license |
| --- | --- |
| **Your laptop, for personal use and experimentation** | Requires a free local Intelligence license. Desktop setup handles this for you. |
| **Kubernetes evaluation** | Requires a free Intelligence trial license. [Request a trial](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=business&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access). |
| **Kubernetes / production** | Requires a production Intelligence license beyond evaluation. OpenBot for Business includes Intelligence for use with OpenBot. [Plans and pricing](https://open.bot/pricing). |

**Fully local is an option.** Run OpenBot, Intelligence, and a compatible model locally. A cloud model or connected online app still sends requests to that service. Initial downloads, account sign-in, and local license renewal need internet access.

---

## Deploy on Kubernetes

Deploy OpenBot and CopilotKit Intelligence together on **AWS EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE, or your own Kubernetes cluster**. The chart installs Intelligence by default; no separate hosted project is required.

For a first evaluation, you need a cluster with **amd64 nodes**, a **default StorageClass**, `kubectl`, Helm, a **trial or production license**, and a model key. The commands below use an OpenAI key. For Anthropic, a model router, cluster sizing, or an existing Intelligence deployment, use the full Helm guide that comes with the chart (`helm show readme` on the chart below).

> **Setting up with an AI assistant?** Give it this README and the Helm guide (`helm show readme` on the chart below). The guide covers cloud-specific values, storage, secrets, sign-in, networking, upgrades, and troubleshooting. Use the evaluation below only through a local port-forward; configure sign-in and TLS before sharing a deployment.

1. **Create `openbot-values.yaml` locally.** Replace the placeholders with your license and model key. Keep this file out of source control.

   ```yaml
   config:
     singleUser: true
   postgresql:
     enabled: true
   secrets:
     licenseToken: "<your CopilotKit trial or production license>"
     modelApiKey: "<your OpenAI API key>"
   ```

2. **Install** the chart published with the release.

   ```sh
   helm install openbot https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot/releases/download/v1.0.2/openbot-0.2.0.tgz \
     --namespace openbot --create-namespace \
     --values openbot-values.yaml \
     --timeout 15m
   ```

3. **Open your evaluation.**

   ```sh
   kubectl -n openbot get pods,jobs
   kubectl -n openbot port-forward svc/openbot-server 3001:3001
   ```

   Open <http://127.0.0.1:3001>. This configuration is single-user: anyone who can reach it is an administrator. Keep the port-forward local.

The chart creates the runtime credentials, installs the databases, bootstraps Intelligence, and sets up the Learning container and scheduled jobs. Automatic Learning uses your model key too.

For a team deployment, follow the Helm guide (`helm show readme` on the chart) to configure authentication, TLS, your database, secrets, persistent storage, and network policies. For a single-container alternative, see [Deploy it](#deploy-it).

## Run from source

Use the template to customize the workspace, branding, Bots, and skills. The source setup below uses managed Intelligence by default; [local Intelligence](#intelligence-on-your-own-machine) is also available.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot.git
cd OpenBot
```

### Requirements

To run the open-source template locally, you’ll need the following.

- Docker, for PostgreSQL, the API server and the shipped Bots. The server, its routine worker and
  the Bots' computers run from the published OpenBot images, which `scripts/start.sh` pulls at the
  tag in `backend-images.env`: `main` in a checkout of `main`, the images built from main, and the
  release's own version in a release (`v1.0.3` in the v1.0.3 tag). Nothing else is built or needed
  for them.
- [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.4+, for the app, the setup helpers and the tests (some tests fail on 1.3).
- A CopilotKit Intelligence project and license. A free plan is available, and Intelligence can be self-hosted.
- A model key. The proof-of-concept Bot uses OpenAI; the LangGraph Bot can use OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google.

### Quick start

The example configuration sets `OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true`, so you can try the app as a local administrator. Configure [sign-in](#sign-in) before giving anyone else access. On a Mac, the free Developer plan also covers [running Intelligence locally](#intelligence-on-your-own-machine) with Docker.

> **Setting up with an AI assistant?** Paste [`prompt.txt`](prompt.txt) into it first. It carries the
> same steps as below plus the things that are easy to get wrong: which of the blank keys in
> `.env.example` are actually yours to fill (the CopilotKit key and a model key), which the start
> script fills for you, and what each start-up refusal means. Every claim in it is checked against
> this repository.

1. Create `.env`:

   ```sh
   cp .env.example .env
   bun install
   ```

2. Connect a fresh managed Intelligence project:

   ```sh
   npx --yes copilotkit@latest login
   npx --yes copilotkit@latest project select
   bun scripts/setup-learning.ts
   ```

   The helper provisions the selected project's runtime key, creates or reuses its
   `openbot` Learning container, then writes both settings to `.env`. It preserves
   custom container assignments and never replaces an existing OpenBot key; with one
   set, it only creates `openbot` in that key's project if it is missing.
   For fresh self-hosted setup, set `INTELLIGENCE_API_URL` to that deployment's
   HTTPS API origin (or `http://localhost` for a local one) and run the helper
   without the two `npx` commands. It opens an isolated Chrome or Edge window for
   your usual sign-in and project choice; install either browser first. For CLI-managed
   local evaluation installs, it discovers the matching dashboard with the newest installed or
   cached CopilotKit CLI and uses that dashboard for login and session requests. Discovery
   runs offline with Bun, without downloading the CLI or requiring `npx` on your PATH.
   If no CLI is available, manually hosted deployments use their API origin for sign-in. Complete the local auth
   approval shown in the browser when prompted. The runtime API URL stays unchanged. It writes
   the API URL, the key and the container, not `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL`, so
   set that one to the same deployment yourself. Once `openbot` exists, the server assigns it
   as the default by itself unless [Admin → Automatic Learning](docs/automatic-learning.md)
   has a saved setting.
   Managed Intelligence needs no separate license token.

   The same CopilotKit CLI sign-in provisions Composio automatically when you run
   `bash scripts/start.sh`. If that cannot complete, OpenBot still starts, with apps
   unavailable. You can run `bun run setup:composio` first to prepare it separately, or
   later to retry; it does not need a Learning container. The helper creates or reuses one
   isolated Composio project for this installation and saves its project key to `.env`.
   Existing Composio keys and Arcade configurations are preserved. Keep the private
   `.env.openbot-installation-id` file across restarts and interrupted setup attempts;
   do not copy it into a new installation. This needs a published CopilotKit CLI with
   `integrations composio provision` and the hosted provisioning service enabled.
   See [Composio setup](docs/plugins/composio.md#automatic-project-setup) for deployment preparation.

3. Fill the remaining required values:

   - `OPENAI_API_KEY`

   Keep the managed Intelligence URLs from `.env.example` unless you run Intelligence yourself. The example `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is public and fine locally; generate your own with:

   ```sh
   openssl rand -base64 32
   ```

4. Run:

   ```sh
   bash scripts/start.sh
   ```

5. Open <http://localhost:3010>.

`scripts/start.sh` pulls the OpenBot images at the tag in `backend-images.env`, starts Docker services, applies migrations, starts the API server on port 3001 and the routine worker from the OpenBot server image, starts the app from this checkout on port 3010, and checks that the services answer their own health routes before printing next steps. It pulls on every start, so a checkout of `main` runs the images built from main now; offline, it uses the copies already on the machine. The server's log is `docker compose logs server`.

`scripts/stop.sh` takes the same things down, including each Bot's computer, which compose does not own; `--keep-computers` leaves the computers running. Nothing is deleted: the database, the Bots' files and their browser profiles are volumes.

### On Windows

Run the clone inside WSL 2 with Ubuntu, and run every step above from an Ubuntu terminal.
[Windows (WSL 2)](docs/development.md#windows-wsl-2) lists what to install in Ubuntu first. Keep an
Ubuntu terminal open while you use OpenBot, and open the app from your Windows browser at
<http://127.0.0.1:3010>.

### Intelligence on your own machine

To try Intelligence on one Mac instead of the managed service, follow
[Evaluate Intelligence locally](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/intelligence/self-hosting-local). The free
[Developer plan](https://www.copilotkit.ai/pricing) qualifies. The local license lasts 30 days and
`npx copilotkit@latest local renew` renews it as often as you need, while your account is in good

# A2UI

**Build delightful, fast, reliable agentic experiences**

A2UI (Agent-to-User Interface) is an open-source generative UI framework,
complete with a protocol optimized for streaming dynamic user interfaces at
low latency, native renderers for web and mobile frameworks, and agent SDKs
in several popular languages. With A2UI, your agents can communicate with
your users using natively rendered widgets, in addition to text.

<img src="docs/assets/a2ui_gallery_examples.png" alt="Gallery of A2UI components" height="400">

_Examples of UI compositions that A2UI can express._

## Quick links

- [Main website](https://a2ui.org).
- Try it in your browser using [A2UI Composer](https://a2ui-project.github.io/composer/).
- [Supported renderers](https://a2ui.org/reference/renderers/).
- [Supported agents](https://a2ui.org/reference/agents/).
- [Protocol specification](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/).

## Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) and decision models (e.g.
[Jev](https://docs.typesafe.ai/)) excel at creating text and code and at making
fast decisions on top of raw structured data (e.g. JSON). A2UI gives these
models a specialized vocabulary for expressing user interfaces.

A2UI expresses UI using _data_, not code. A schema for the data exchanged
between the agent and the renderer enforces strict capability boundaries for
the agent, keeping agent-generated experiences safe and aligned with the
business requirements of your application. A _core library_, a _native
framework adapter_, and a _catalog of components_ provide access to native
components and form the building blocks that the agent _composes_ into a final
user experience, making the result expressive and high-performance.

## When to use A2UI

Use A2UI when any of the following apply to your application:

- Parts of your application are agent- and/or server-driven. By design, A2UI
  supports remote rendering.
- You want the UI to be composed dynamically, tailored to the user's immediate
  need. Instead of making your users navigate through multiple screens to solve
  their problems, have the agent build the right flow of UI that guides users
  directly to solutions.
- You need the highest performance and visual fidelity. A2UI renders UI using
  the framework of your choice, typically one that the host app itself is
  written in. WebViews or HTML are not required.
- The same agent streams UI to multiple platforms or frameworks, such as
  Flutter, React, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose. A2UI helps keep the user
  experience compatible and consistent across all screens.
- The agent is remote, third-party, or operates across a trust boundary. For
  example, the agent must not be able to handle certain kinds of data (credit
  card/account numbers, PII, financial data). A2UI helps enforce the trust
  boundary and protect your app's critical functionality from hallucinations
  using a strict schema, and by expressing UI using validated data rather than
  executable code.

## A2UI core philosophy

We develop A2UI under the guidance of the following core principles:

- **Security first**: The app developer controls what the agent can and cannot
  do in the app. A2UI provides a framework for specifying and enforcing the
  necessary guardrails, such as expressing UI as data, validating inputs and
  outputs against a schema, and disallowing arbitrary executable code. Every
  capability granted to the agent is either a safe standard capability built
  into the framework, or a capability explicitly granted by the app developer.
- **Model-friendly and server-driven**: The A2UI protocol is designed to be
  efficiently generated by language and decision models and transported over
  the network, and to support progressive rendering (or "streaming") for a
  responsive user experience. An agent can adapt the UI based on where the user
  takes the conversation. A2UI supports swappable inference formats, so you can
  tailor inference to specific models and use cases.
- **Native rendering and portability**: A2UI renders UI using the framework
  native to your app, with renderers for many major UI frameworks. No need to
  change frameworks unless required for other reasons.

## Architecture

A2UI's architecture is made of multiple layers spanning the full stack that
connects the agent to the application:

1. **Inference**: An agent (typically backed by a language or a decision model)
   instructed by an A2UI skill (created using an A2UI Agent SDK) generates the
   description of UI and data using an appropriate inference format (e.g. A2UI
   Express, or a decision tree).
2. **Transport**: An A2UI Agent SDK, embedded in a larger agent architecture,
   parses and validates the model's output, expands macros, and converts the UI
   to the wire-stable _A2UI Transport_ protocol messages, which are sent to the
   renderer.
3. **Rendering**: A renderer is made of an _A2UI Core_ library (e.g. the
   `@a2ui/web_core` npm package, or `a2ui_core` Dart package), a UI framework
   adapter (e.g. `@a2ui/react` React adapter, or `a2ui_flutter` Flutter
   adapter), and a widget catalog. The core library parses the incoming
   messages and creates a framework-agnostic in-memory representation of the UI
   and data. The framework adapter maps the in-memory representation to concrete
   framework-specific UI widgets. The widget catalog provides access to the
   widgets the agent is allowed to compose.

## Getting started

Pick the path that matches where you want to start:

| Path                                                             | What you get                                                                                                    | Time   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------ |
| 🍜 **[Quickstart](https://a2ui.org/quickstart/)**                | A full-stack A2UI app with a backend and frontend. Learn A2UI end-to-end and customize to your use case.        | ~5 min |
| 🎨 **[A2UI Composer](https://a2ui-project.github.io/composer/)** | Generate A2UI JSON from a visual editor and paste it into any agent prompt — no install required.               | ~1 min |
| 🎬 **[A2UI Theater](https://a2ui-composer.ag-ui.com/theater)**   | Step through pre-built A2UI streaming scenarios across Lit, React, and Angular renderers — no install required. | ~1 min |

## Packages

These packages are developed in this repository. Packages marked "Not published
yet" can be used from source.

| [a2ui-agent-sdk](python/a2ui_agent/) | Agent SDK: negotiates catalogs, generates prompts and skills, and compiles model output into A2UI. | [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/a2ui-agent-sdk.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/a2ui-agent-sdk/) |
| [a2ui-a2a](python/a2ui_a2a/)         | Connects the agent SDK to the [Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org).           | [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/a2ui-a2a.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/a2ui-a2a/)             |
| [a2ui-adk](python/a2ui_adk/)         | Connects the agent SDK to the [Agent Development Kit (ADK)](https://github.com/google/adk-python). | [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/a2ui-adk.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/a2ui-adk/)             |

### TypeScript

## Roadmap

- **Protocol v1.1**: We are collecting requirements for the next iteration of
  the A2UI protocol.
- **Inference**: Support for decision models (e.g. Jev).
- **Templates**: A cross-framework templating engine and a set of standard
  primitives for rendering reusable rich UI widgets.
- **Sandboxed logic**: A way to securely attach logic to A2UI components.
- **Agent SDK**: Skill generation, better diagnostics, and integrations with
  more agent frameworks.
- **Evals**: A set of tools for evaluating generated UI quality.
- **MCP Apps**: Embedding MCP Apps inside A2UI, and embedding A2UI experiences
  into MCP Apps.
- **CLI**: Schema validation, codegen, local preview, and integration with
  coding agents.

## Contribute

A2UI is an **Apache 2.0** licensed project. We believe the future of UI is agentic,
and we want to work with you to help build it.

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for details on how to get started.

# Locally Uncensored

**The all-in-one local AI studio for your desktop. Chat, images, video and a coding agent in one app. Install it, pick a model, go.**

Free and open source. In local mode everything runs on your own machine. No Docker, no terminal, no config files. The platforms are listed under [Download](#download).

## Download

Take the latest build from [Releases](https://github.com/PurpleDoubleD/locally-uncensored/releases/latest).

| Linux | [`Locally.Uncensored_3.0.10_amd64.AppImage`](https://github.com/PurpleDoubleD/locally-uncensored/releases/latest/download/Locally.Uncensored_3.0.10_amd64.AppImage), [`Locally.Uncensored_3.0.10_amd64.deb`](https://github.com/PurpleDoubleD/locally-uncensored/releases/latest/download/Locally.Uncensored_3.0.10_amd64.deb) or [`Locally.Uncensored-3.0.10-1.x86_64.rpm`](https://github.com/PurpleDoubleD/locally-uncensored/releases/latest/download/Locally.Uncensored-3.0.10-1.x86_64.rpm) | Built on every release |
| macOS 14 or newer, Apple Silicon (Beta) | [`LU_3.0.10_aarch64.dmg`](https://github.com/PurpleDoubleD/locally-uncensored/releases/download/v3.0.10/LU_3.0.10_aarch64.dmg) | Signed with an Apple Developer ID and notarized by Apple. Intel Macs are not supported. The app has run on one Mac so far. Voice has been tried by hand in the app on a Mac and works. Computer control is in the Mac app but not fully tested yet on macOS. Remote Access and the automatic update are not confirmed on macOS |
| Android 7.0 or newer (arm64) | [`LU-3.0.10-Android.apk`](https://github.com/PurpleDoubleD/locally-uncensored/releases/download/v3.0.10/LU-3.0.10-Android.apk) | The phone app. Not in the Play Store yet: install the file from this page. SHA-256 `dbd515d81bbc8ab70f21b850424f9f8b57ae88ae24962225beefc4116d139d2f` |

<!-- MAC: the macOS row above is the one place in this file that says whether there is a Mac build. This is the Mac version of the row. It is true only for the .dmg that the release run built, signed and notarized, so it goes out after that run is green. -->

Some antivirus engines flag unsigned NSIS installers that download other binaries, which is a false positive. The installer is built by GitHub Actions from the public source on `master`, and the update channel is signed against a public minisign key, so you can verify both: see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md#antivirus--browser-false-positives).

Code signing for the Windows installers: free code signing provided by [SignPath.io](https://about.signpath.io), certificate by [SignPath Foundation](https://signpath.org). SignPath Foundation has accepted the project. The production certificate is not in place yet, and until it is the installers ship unsigned.

Current release: **v3.0.10** (November 2026). Every change since 1.0.0 is in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

3.0.10 fixes lost chats from 3.0.8 and 3.0.9. A backup no longer replaces the only complete copy of your chats, a note at launch says when the backup holds chats that are missing from your list, and Settings, Chat Backup has Restore chats from backup. The Android app is back as an APK, with the keyboard staying open in the Create prompt.

3.0.9 brings Liquid's LFM3 models for small machines: 1.7B and 2B, about 1 to 1.7 GB each, for text, pictures and speech, on the LU Engine, on Ollama or as MLX builds on a Mac; the LU Engine moves to llama.cpp b11960 for them. A group chat now sends every speaker the context you picked, can redo one speaker and lets you set who speaks when. A compaction is one quiet line in the chat, and the conversation before it stays one click away. Animate takes an end image and, with MiniMax H3, up to nine reference pictures, and Krea 2, Qwen-Image 2.1 and FLUX.2 take reference pictures for a style, a person or a pose. Local videos run up to 15 seconds without drifting in colour, and a video shows a rough preview while it renders. The trainer learns a style, a concept or a pose next to a character (Beta). "Use this model" on Hugging Face opens the download in LU, and a model from the search comes in a quant that fits your graphics card. A status menu sits in the Mac menu bar and the Windows and Linux tray, and the Linux AppImage starts again on systems without the tray library. What has only run in automated tests is listed under Known limits in the [release notes](https://github.com/PurpleDoubleD/locally-uncensored/releases/tag/v3.0.9).

3.0.8 makes web search in the chat work again: LU asks five search services in turn and needs no key for any of them. A video made in the chat plays in the chat, and a long one renders in the background while you write on. A picture attached in the chat reaches the image tool, and with two graphics cards chat and ComfyUI can each get their own. The LU Engine plans a model's memory from the file itself and offers a shorter context with one click. AMD cards on Windows get AMD's current ROCm build. New: the chat can read and change LU's settings with a confirmation card, the Model Manager can make a copy of a local model that refuses less, and Settings, Storage puts models, gallery and runtime in one folder of your choice. What has only run in automated tests is listed under Known limits in the [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md).

3.0.5 was about Create: LTX 2.5, FastH3 and YuE2 run on your own machine, Qwen-Image 2.1 gets a transparent background and its prompt enhancer, Edit, Remove Background and Enhance Image take up to 50 images in one go, and LU Cloud adds Qwen Image 2.1, LTX 2.5, MiniMax H3 and Wan 3.0 Reference. Chat takes any file, each model in a group chat can have its own persona, dropdowns stay inside the window (issue 149), and the speech install works again on Ubuntu 24.04.

3.0.4 fixed the Code agent and the agent in chat on LU Cloud: writing a long file no longer ends the run, "continue" picks up where a run stopped instead of starting over, the agent keeps a plan only when you ask for one, and cloud context is 32K by default and can be set per model. It also fixed the bugs reported on GitHub and Discord since 3.0.3 (issues 144 to 147): MiniMax H3 runs as a video model with sound, Edit takes up to three extra images with Qwen-Image 2.1, a missing encoder or VAE is named and offered as a download instead of ending in "Value not in list", the LoRA stack follows the loras folder, and group chat works with every LU Engine model.

3.0.3 was a hotfix: chats with many images no longer run the app out of memory, Create reads a model's family from the file instead of its name, and the five bugs reported on GitHub since 3.0.2 are fixed (issues 139 to 143).

3.0.2 was a hotfix: the Code tab lost its scrollbar and its input box once a conversation grew taller than the window (issue 138, a regression in 3.0.1) and is held to the window height again, and the count of open cloud models now takes the Create Studio endpoints in, which makes it fourteen video models and seven image models.

### What is new in 3.0.1

- **Qwen-Image 2.1 runs locally on Windows and Linux.** One model generates a picture from a prompt and edits one from a reference image, with no mask to paint. About 16 GB of files, ComfyUI 0.37.0 or newer, and a research license that does not allow commercial use.
- **Models has a LoRAs tab of its own.** Search CivitAI, download into ComfyUI's `models/loras` folder, see what is installed with its size and trigger word, and delete what you no longer want.
- **A GPU whose free memory could not be measured is planned more carefully**, and the log now says total capacity instead of calling it free.
- **The Linux AppImage stops handing its own runtime to every program LU starts**, so a healthy system Python, pip, git or ffmpeg keeps working, and a distribution that blocks pip in the system Python keeps the isolated environment LU built.
- **The local model runs one conversation at a time and says so**, with a line showing how many chats are ahead. Stop works while a chat is still waiting.
- **Temperature, Top P and Max tokens belong to the conversation you moved them in**, instead of every open chat sharing one value.
- **Cloud video renders offer the clip lengths the picked model really supports**, read from the live catalog.

## Mobile app (Android, iPhone)

LU is also available as an app for your phone. The current APK comes from the 3.0.10 release.

- **Android:** download `LU-3.0.10-Android.apk` from the [3.0.10 release](https://github.com/PurpleDoubleD/locally-uncensored/releases/tag/v3.0.10). Needs Android 7.0 or newer on a 64-bit (arm64) phone. Allow installing apps from your browser or file app when Android asks. SHA-256: `dbd515d81bbc8ab70f21b850424f9f8b57ae88ae24962225beefc4116d139d2f`
- **iPhone:** in review at the App Store.
- **Google Play:** coming later.

What the app does:
- Run AI models on your phone and chat offline. Chats with on-device models stay on the phone.
- Ask questions about your own documents. Memory and personas.
- Optional LU Cloud with your account: larger hosted chat models, Create (images and video) and dictation.
- Connect to LU on your own computer over your home Wi-Fi and chat with the models on your PC.

Later APKs install over this one and keep your data. The Google Play version will be signed by Google: to switch to it, export your chats first (Settings, Data) and uninstall the APK.

## Three steps

1. **Install.** Run the installer like any other program. On first launch a wizard looks for an AI engine that is already running on your machine, and installs one for you with a single click if there is none. It does the same for ComfyUI, which draws the images and video.
2. **Pick a model.** The model manager marks which models fit your hardware and downloads them in one click. It works with the engine you already have (Ollama, LM Studio and others) and can link models those tools already store, without copying them. Loading a model in Ollama or LM Studio can be cancelled, and an Ollama model that runs partly on the processor says so.
3. **Create.** Chat, Create, Code and Agent are tabs in one window. Type in one, switch to the next, keep the same models.

Walkthrough with screenshots: [Getting started guide](https://locallyuncensored.com/guide/). New to local AI: [the five minute beginner guide](https://locallyuncensored.com/blog/how-to-run-ai-locally.html).

<details>
<summary><strong>Build from source, or contribute</strong></summary>

```bash
git clone https://github.com/PurpleDoubleD/locally-uncensored.git
cd locally-uncensored
npm install
npm run dev          # browser dev mode
npm run tauri build  # desktop binary
```

`setup.bat` on Windows and `setup.sh` on Linux and macOS bootstrap Node, Git and Ollama for dev mode. See the [contributing guide](CONTRIBUTING.md).

</details>

## What is in the box

**Chat.** Models that answer directly, without refusals, next to the mainstream ones in the same menu. Thinking is shown as it happens, with an effort control on the models that offer one. Upload an image and ask about it (a local model with image input is downloaded together with its image part, the second file it needs to see pictures), chat with your own documents through a local index, talk instead of typing and have answers read back, keep a memory across conversations, switch personas, and import your ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini export so the old threads come with you. A long conversation folds its older turns into a summary instead of running out of room.

**Create.** Images and video on your own GPU through a ComfyUI the app installs, starts, repairs and updates for you. No node graphs. The lanes are text to image, edit and image to image with a mask for inpainting, remove background, video, animate an image, extend a clip, motion control, talking character, music, and Character Studio, which trains a character on your own card and drops it into your local LoRA folder. A LoRA picker with a stack and strength sliders reads the folder live, and everything you make lands in the gallery. Upscale and Erase Object are the two lanes that run in the cloud only. [How it works](https://locallyuncensored.com/blog/easiest-local-ai-image-generator.html).

**Code.** A coding agent that builds a map of the repo, edits only the lines you asked for, shows the diff before it applies anything, runs your tests and reads the failures, and carries typed git tools and per project rules in a `.lurules` file. Ask, Plan and Bypass modes per conversation, a file explorer with preview, and a workspace per project. A Local API in Settings puts every local model on one OpenAI compatible address behind a token, so your other coding tools can use the same machine.

**Agent.** Web search and fetch, reading and writing files, a shell, code execution, screenshots, image and video generation, and your own MCP servers on top. Long jobs go to background agents that work while you carry on, and a panel shows what is running. Every tool call passes a permission gate you control, and a read only run stays read only.

**Voice (Beta).** A spoken conversation with the chat model you picked. Speech recognition, the voice and the turn taking run on your own machine, in English, with fifteen voices. You can interrupt an answer by speaking, the model can use the agent tools with the same permissions, and you decide whether those tools reach your workspace folder or the whole computer. Voice runs in local mode only, and with the Cloud switch on it is hidden. Voice is in beta: it is new, and your computer may still show rough edges. Our check in the real app ran on Windows, and on a Mac Voice has been tried by hand in the app. [VOICE.md](VOICE.md) has the setup and what was measured.

**Computer control (Beta).** A model looks at the screen and uses the mouse and the keyboard in apps you approve. It is off until you switch it on, asks once in every new chat before it starts, asks before every action unless you make a session autonomous, and never touches terminals, password managers or password fields. Anything that sends, buys or deletes needs your click, and so does a button without a name. In an autonomous session, moving the mouse pauses it, and a shortcut stops it at any time. It is in beta: it is new and not proven in every app yet, so watch what it does and stop it when it goes wrong. Our check in the real app ran on Windows. On a Mac it is in the app but not fully tested yet. [COMPUTER-CONTROL.md](COMPUTER-CONTROL.md) lists what it asks and what it never touches.

**Everywhere.** Reach the app from your phone over your LAN or through a Cloudflare tunnel, paired by QR code and a passcode, off until you turn it on, with connected devices listed. Compare two models side by side, benchmark them on your own hardware for speed, cost and correctness, and take updates over a signed channel. [Phone details](https://locallyuncensored.com/blog/local-ai-on-your-phone.html).


## Optional: LU Labs Cloud

Some models are larger than any desktop card. Flip the Cloud switch in the same app and those run on hosted GPUs instead, with the heavy Create lanes alongside them. The same account works in the browser at [lu-labs.ai](https://lu-labs.ai), on a plan or on credit packs that do not expire. The local app stays free either way, and switching back to local costs nothing: [plans and prices](https://lu-labs.ai/pricing). With Create in chat (Beta), a cloud chat model can put together an order for images, video, music or voice, and nothing runs until you approve it.

Since 3.0.0 the catalogue says what it can back up. Every cloud chat model was asked the same two questions twice and judged on the answer, and a longer three-round test on 2026-10-05 took the mark from five more: 19 of the 46 we measured answer in full, and only those carry the No Filter mark in the picker. Across all measured answers, 5% were refusals. Ten more chat models that their makers release to answer without refusing are listed as a group of their own, marked Uncensored (Beta). They were not part of the measurement above. On an active plan, 11 models on Hosted and 12 on Pro and Max cost no credits in chat, up to a daily limit. For images and video, 14 video and 7 image models run without a built-in content restriction, most of them with Uncensored in the name, and your account decides what they may produce.

# 🎨 dsh-image-gen

### 在 DeepSeek Harness 里，用说话的方式画图

<p><b>对话批量生图 · GIF 动图 · 看得懂草图的 AI 画布 · Agent 自动套用 500+ Prompt 灵感 · 订阅账号免 Key</b></p>

<p>
